newsitem.title: USA: Local phone cos could feel pinch from FCC ruling.
newsitem.headline: Local phone cos could feel pinch from FCC ruling.

text.p: Local phone companies could feel a short-term pinch from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission ruling Wednesday that reduces the access charges paid to the local providers by long distance firms.
The FCC, which adopted landmark rules today to increase competition and lower prices in the $200 billion a year phone industry, voted to reduce the access charges by $18.5 billion over five years.
This cut would mean less money immediately available for the universal service fund which provides phone services to rural areas and possibly more burden on the regional Bells.
"It does disadvantage some of the local phone companies because they use some of the access charges to pay for universal service," said Randy Carlson, a senior analyst at the Yankee Group.
"What they are probably going to end up doing is shrinking the universal service funds and that will probably impact the service the rural customers get," he said.

The FCC rulings stem from the telecommunications law passed last year that has unleashed a competitive frenzy for market share, with the long distance companies poised to enter the local markets while local players and newcomers are eager to offer long-distance competition.
Jeffrey Kagan, president of Kagan Telecom Associates, said the FCC had a nearly impossible task of issuing these rules, facing pressure from Congress, consumers, and phone companies.

"They needed to try to level a playing field that can't be made level. So now the Baby Bells think the FCC went too far, while the long distance companies think they didn't go far enough," Kagan said.
Kagan estimated that the ruling's long-term effects will be minimal on the regional Bells, as they expand into the long distance arena.

"If you go out a few years, they are all going to be in the same business," Kagan said. "Baby Bells will be selling discounted long distance service and the long distance companies will be discounting local service."
Analyst and companies alike said they would withhold final judgement on the ruling until they see the full FCC orders, which will not be available for at least a week.
"A lot of time the devil is in the details. These things are not 700 pages long just for the fun of it," Prudential analyst Guy Woodlief said.
In the meantime, most of the seven regional Bell companies and GTE Corp said they are not happy.
U S West Communications Group said the FCC "turned its back" on much of rural America because of the higher access charges.

Bell Atlantic Corp and NYNEX Corp said they were "...disappointed that the FCC has gone beyond the requirements of the Telecom Act by mandating lower access charges rather than letting the market drive down prices."
Meanwhile, AT&T Corp's chairman and chief executive, Robert Allen, said he considered the ruling a "good compromise."

"Today's action is a significant first step -- but only a first step -- in what we expect will be an on-going process to reduce the inflated access fees we pay to the monopoly local telephone companies," Allen said.
